title: Storage and initial processing of water samples for organic carbon analysis in runoff
author: Nachimuthu, Watkins, et al.

steps.title: Collect water samples
steps.instruction: Collect 14 water samples (71 % runoff, 29 % irrigation) from two irrigation events in a cotton field on 8 Dec 2015 and 31 Dec 2015.

steps.title: Create refrigerated and frozen subsamples
steps.instruction: Immediately after collection split each sample into two aliquots: store one set at 4 °C (refrigerator) and the other set at –18 °C (freezer).

steps.title: Transport samples to laboratory
steps.instruction: Transport all aliquots to the laboratory and keep them at their respective storage temperatures until analysis on 21 Jan 2016.

steps.title: Filter samples for DOC
steps.instruction: For DOC determination, filter the appropriate aliquot through a 0.45 µm filter that does not contain dissolved carbon fractions.

substeps.instruction: If samples were frozen, allow them to thaw overnight at ~20 °C before filtering.

steps.title: Acidify to remove inorganic carbon
steps.instruction: Acidify each filtered (for DOC) and unfiltered (for TOC) sample to pH < 2 to purge inorganic carbon as CO₂.

steps.title: Oxidize carbon with heated persulfate
steps.instruction: Perform persulfate oxidation on both filtered (DOC) and unfiltered (TOC) samples by heating to 116–130 °C according to the American Public Health Association Method.

steps.title: Measure TOC and DOC concentrations
steps.instruction: Analyze the oxidized filtrate for dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and the oxidized unfiltered sample for total organic carbon (TOC).

steps.title: Determine total suspended solids
steps.instruction: Mix each well‑sampleed water, filter up to 100 mL through a pre‑weighed 47 mm diameter Macherey‑Nagel MN GF‑3 glass‑fiber filter, dry the filter at 105 °C for a minimum of 24 h, and calculate TSS from the weight gain.

description: The relationship between frozen and cold storage samples were tested using linear regression. The storage method validation results indicate that frozen TOC and DOC values were generally higher than unfrozen sample TOC concentrations (Fig. 1) suggesting a degradation or loss mechanisms occurring during 4 °C storage. The DOC as a fraction of TOC generally differed when frozen, but the effect was inconsistent. The DOC varied from 86 to 100% of TOC within frozen samples and 53 to 100% of TOC within fresh samples. TSS concentration doesn't explain this inconsistent effect (supplementary figure 1 and 2). However, there was clear evidence that freezing and thawing (frozen samples were left overnight at room temperature (~20 °C before analysis or filtering) affected DOC concentrations. We suggest, therefore, that water samples should be filtered for DOC analysis before storage in the freezer and unfiltered samples used for TOC analysis should be frozen immediately after collection. Storing the water samples in the refrigerator (4 °C) lead to a decline in both TOC and DOC concentrations. A confirmatory study was also conducted on the effect on storage time on the decline in TOC and DOC concentrations as described below.Fig. 1Relationship between (A) TOC (mg/L) and (B) DOC (mg/L) of frozen and unfrozen (fresh) samples.
